subject: environmental-science

moments.title: Flint water crisis begins
moments.body: In April 2014, the city of Flint (majority Black, 41% below poverty line) switches its water source from Detroit to the Flint River as a cost-cutting measure under state-appointed emergency management. Corrosion control is not added. Lead from old pipes leaches into drinking water. Officials deny the problem for over a year. Marc Edwards (Virginia Tech) and Dr Mona Hanna-Attisha (paediatrician) document elevated blood lead levels in children.
moments.takeaway: Cost-cutting on a public utility produced a documented public health disaster in a majority-Black US city in 2014-15.

now.title: Lead in water today
now.body: EPA's Lead and Copper Rule revisions (2024) require replacement of all lead service lines within 10 years. Estimated 9 million US homes have lead pipes. Many other countries — UK, France, Canada — have similar legacies. Lead exposure remains a global environmental health issue.
now.open_questions: Will lead pipe replacement be funded at the required scale? The 2021 US infrastructure law allocated $15bn — less than needed.

reflection: Flint became a case study in environmental justice: which communities get clean water depends on race, income and political voice. Robert Bullard's 'Dumping in Dixie' (1990) had named this pattern 25 years earlier.
